input:
In this worked example, we are going to determine the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe, and then use the result to say whether the flow is laminar or turbulent. The pipe has a diameter of 0.025 m, and the water flows with a mean velocity of 1.1 m s-1. It turns out that the Reynolds number is large enough that the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number, usually written as Re, is a dimensionless quantity that is calculated from four properties of the flow: the density rho, which is measured in kg m-3, the mean velocity v, measured in m s-1, the pipe diameter D, measured in m, and the dynamic viscosity mu, measured in Pa s. The relationship is Re = rho v D / mu. For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is equal to 998 kg m-3, and the dynamic viscosity mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s.

If we substitute the numbers into the relationship, we get Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. To interpret this, it is helpful to remember that flow is regarded as laminar when the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, and as turbulent when it is above Re = 4000. For values in between, the regime is described as transitional, and the number by itself does not settle which regime applies. In the present case the calculated value of 27400 lies far above the upper of the two thresholds, so the flow can be classified as turbulent with some confidence.
target:
The Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe of diameter 0.025 m at a mean velocity of 1.1 m s-1 is 27400, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Each quantity is taken at the stated temperature.

Substitution of the values gives Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000. Between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, and the regime is turbulent. The number compares the inertial effect of the flow with the viscous effect at the wall; a large value marks a flow in which viscosity no longer orders the motion across the whole section. The thresholds used here are the pipe-flow thresholds, and the assignment is made for the stated diameter and velocity only; a change in either moves the value and can move the regime across a threshold.
